01.r: Joins this verse to the list of what the king will take; the object marker points to 'your fields'.
01.n: The Hebrew is 'and' with the small word that marks a definite direct object, which has no English equivalent; both are counted here with 'your fields'.

02.r: The ploughed land of each family.
02.n: Gesenius gives the first sense as a plain, a level tract, and then a field. The list stands first, before its verb, so the stress falls on what is taken.

03.r: Adds the next item; the object marker again points to it.
03.n: 'And' with the object marker, as before 'your fields'.

04.n: Gesenius gives the first sense as a field set with plants of nobler quality, cultivated as a garden or orchard, and notes the phrase 'a vineyard of olives' for an olive yard.

05.r: The olive trees that give each family its oil.
05.n: The Hebrew says simply 'your olives'; BDB: olive tree, olive. The Geneva says 'Oliue trees'.

06.r: The king takes the best land, not the poorest.
06.n: Literally 'the good ones'; Gesenius notes the physical sense, good as in fertile land. It may describe all three items or only the olives: the KJV reads all three ('even the best of them'), the Geneva and DRC only the olives.

07.r: The king will take the land from its owners.
07.n: The same common verb for 'take' that runs through Samuel's list.

08.r: He passes the land on to his own men.
08.n: A perfect with 'and', carrying on the future before it; YLT renders it literally, 'hath given'. Gesenius: to give, followed by 'to' of the person. The Hebrew gives no object; most translations add 'them'.

09.r: The king's men who serve him at court.
09.n: The word means a slave or servant; Gesenius notes that it is applied to the servants of a king, that is, his ministers. Here the context is royal service, so 'servants' rather than 'slaves'.

_extra.7: ἃς: a feminine relative pronoun where the article τοὺς would be expected; likely a slip in the text as given, with nothing in the Hebrew answering to it.
